podcast.body: Between 1984 and 1985, Frankie Goes to Hollywood achieved millions of sales by issuing at least 13 different versions of this single, demonstrating a highly effective strategy for encouraging multiple purchases of the same song through remixes. "In 1984 and 1985, they managed to get people to buy millions of copies of at least 13 different versions of Relax."

podcast.body: This "monstrous single" was first released on October 23, 1983, and its enduring popularity meant it was continually re-released in various forms and mixes, consistently re-entering the charts and generating significant revenue for the band through "successful recycling." "Their monstrous single first released on October 23, 1983."

podcast.body: This debut single was released in 1984 and quickly became embroiled in controversy. The song and its associated hype were characterized by themes of drugs and anonymous bathhouse sex, further emphasized by newspaper ads featuring Holly Johnson in a sailor's cap with the caption, "all the nice boys love seamen." Its commercial performance was initially sluggish until DJ Mike Reed initiated an on-air diatribe, leading the BBC to ban the song for "obscene, homo erotic overtones." This ban ironically propelled the single to number one on the charts, making it one of the most recognizable songs of the entire 1980s. "The newspaper ads for the record featured Holly in a sailor's cap and a leather vest with the caption, all the nice boys love sea men."

podcast.body: The distinctive sound of this song, particularly its snare drum, would not have been possible without the use of the Fairlight Computer Musical Instrument. The snare drum sound is a sample from a Led Zeppelin record, triggered and slightly manipulated in the studio when the drummer hit a snare. "Frank E. Ues to Hollywood and Relax from 1984. The sound on that song would have never been possible without using this new device called a Fairlight."
